note: Proposed, not sealed. Written by the willow fleet seat while closing the G2-meta-scans-nestor bite of the fleet loop plan (Wave 2: port homestead-ledger's meta-scan, re-grounded against this repo's 172 test files). The rule was copied from the sibling, not re-derived; where it reported a helper of this repo's, the helper got a plant in its own file rather than the rule an exemption.

decisions.question: This suite carries dozens of test helpers that read source and judge it — AST walks, regex scans, read_text plus a membership question. Nothing checked that any of them had ever been shown to fire on a planted violation; test_import_hygiene.py and test_version.py plant theirs by hand, most do not. Should there be a test that reads the other test files and holds every scan-shaped helper to a planted-violation test in the same file?
decisions.commitment: Yes: tests/test_scans_fire.py, ported from homestead-ledger's tests/test_scans_fire.py with its discovery rule and plant rule kept verbatim. Discovery is structural (parses or walks source; matches a pattern; reads a file and asks membership of it; walks a module-level word list; filters the caller's terms by membership) with the repo's own name stems on top, so a public `offenders(text)` and a `_run_decision_check` are found by what they do or what they are called, not by a leading underscore. A helper counts as planted only when a test whose name carries plant/fires/catches, or whose docstring carries plant, actually calls it — directly or through the module's own helpers. The meta-scan is itself planted: every discovery shape and every plant-rule edge has a tmp_path fixture that must be reported or must be cleared, and a real file of this repo's (test_version.py) is the control. On the day it landed it reported eleven helpers in seven files; each got a same-file plant in this PR.
decisions.why: A scan that has never fired has not been shown to check anything — the repo already says so in three places (test_import_hygiene.py's docstring, the #292 plant, decision 0127's 'silence from a check means nothing') and enforced it nowhere. Every one of the eleven was a guard some other test trusted: the env-var gates stand on _env_names_in_code, the anchor gates on slugify, the key tests on _is_key_hex, the ledger refusal tests on _tamper_first_line_kind. One of them, test_the_guard_can_fail in test_prompt_advisories_are_reachable.py, was a plant in name only — it asserted a set literal it had built and never called the helper it was named for — which is the exact counter-example the sibling's meta-scan plants, found live here. Copying the sibling's rule rather than writing one is deliberate: a meta-scan that disagreed between repos about what counts as planted would be the drift the fleet loop exists to close.

decisions.question: The same port finds fifty-five test bodies that are themselves inline scans — they read a real file and judge it in place, with no helper to name and so nothing to plant. Homestead factored its own out in a separate bite. Zero is not reachable in this PR; an allowlist would excuse them; an xfail would quarantine the test. How is the inline half held?
decisions.commitment: A shrink-only ledger, INLINE_SCAN_LEDGER, of the fifty-five test ids as found, and one test with two assertions: no offender outside the ledger (a new inline scan anywhere in tests/ fails today), and no ledger entry that has stopped offending (a refactored, renamed or removed test must be struck, or the same test fails). A third test holds every entry to an existing file so a typo cannot sit in the ledger looking like a debt. The PR body names all fifty-five as the follow-up; the day the ledger is empty the test collapses to `assert not offenders`.
decisions.why: The sibling's own docstring warns that a meta-scan that cries wolf 'gets an allowlist bolted to it and stops meaning anything'. What makes an allowlist meaningless is that it only grows and excuses whatever is on it. This ledger can only shrink and excuses nothing: every entry is named as owing a plant, growth is refused, and staleness is refused, so it records the debt exactly rather than hiding it. An xfail was rejected because it would silence the rule wholesale — a fifty-sixth inline scan would land unreported — and because the repo's standing rule is never to skip, disable or quarantine a test to get green. Keeping the rule and ledgering the debt is the smallest honest state: the check runs on every file, today, and says exactly what it found.

decisions.question: Several of the eleven are reported by the name-stem half of the rule or by a shape that is not obviously a scan — _run_decision_check by the stem 'check', _tamper_first_line_kind by read_text plus an `in`, slugify and fenced by a regex call. Should the rule be narrowed so these are not reported, or should they be planted?
decisions.commitment: Planted, every one, in the same file, with a test that shows the helper fires on a planted input and does not fire on the control. Where the helper read a hard-coded path (_env_names_in_code over nestor/, _invoked_actions over .claude/settings.json, _prompt_advisory_modules over hooks/, runnable_examples over README) it gained an optional parameter defaulting to that path so the plant can hand it a file it wrote; no caller changed. The rule was not narrowed and no name was exempted.
decisions.why: Each of these is trusted by the tests around it exactly as a scan is — the ledger refusal tests are only meaningful if the tamper helper actually breaks the chain in a way a size check cannot see; the anchor gates are only meaningful if slugify gets the em dash right, which its own docstring says it once did not. A plant costs one fixture; a narrower rule costs the next helper of the same shape its plant. The sibling's rule was kept verbatim ('keep the rule, re-derive nothing') so the two repos cannot disagree about what counts, and the cheaper honest option — show it fires — was taken for every helper it reported.
